# tshark-mcp

> Read-only MCP server that lets an agent analyse existing packet captures with tshark. Seventeen tools return compact JSON for Diameter, GTPv2-C, GTPv1-C, GTP-U, SIP and SCTP/M3UA/SCCP/TCAP/MAP, pair requests with answers, name result codes and flag what never got a reply. It cannot capture, write, export, resolve names or load code.

## What it can and cannot do

- Reads capture files that already exist inside directories the operator allowed with `--allow-dir`. Every path an agent passes must resolve (symlinks followed) inside one of them; anything else is refused before the file is looked at.
- Every call is bounded: file size (500 MB), matching packets dissected in full (500 per call), frames read per tshark run (200 000), JSON returned (200 KB, rows are dropped and `truncated: true` is set), tshark run time (60 s), files opened by one multi-file call (50).
- tshark is started with an argv list, never a shell, always with `-n` (no name resolution) and `-r` (read a file). Capture, write, export and extension flags are refused before a process starts.
- Display filters are linted and compiled against an empty capture before touching the real file. Field names must exist in `tshark -G fields`.
- Failures come back as `{"error": {"type": ..., "message": ...}}`, never as exceptions.
- A capture that ends mid-packet is read up to the damage; the result then carries `warnings`.
- Every call is written to a JSON-lines audit log when `--log-file` is set.
- Supported transport: stdio. `--transport streamable-http` exists for local experiments only and has no authentication.

## Tools

- `find_identifier(path, identifier, kind="auto", max_files=20)`: which files in a directory mention an IMSI, MSISDN, IP address, SIP Call-ID or Diameter Session-Id; hit counts, first/last timestamps, protocol breakdown per file. Call this first when you do not know which capture to open.
- `pcap_info(path)`: packet count, duration, first/last timestamp, link type, protocol hierarchy, active limits. Call this first on a file.
- `conversations(path, layer="ip", filter=None, limit=200)`: top talkers at ip, ipv6, tcp, udp, sctp or eth, optionally restricted by a display filter.
- `filter_packets(path, display_filter, fields=None, limit=200)`: rows of fields for packets matching a display filter; the escape hatch for anything the protocol tools do not cover.
- `diameter_sessions(path, session_id=None, imsi=None, command_code=None, filter=None, limit=200)`: Diameter grouped by Session-Id with the paired transactions, result codes, unanswered and failed counts.
- `diameter_transactions(path, filter=None, limit=200)`: every Diameter request paired with its answer by Hop-by-Hop id.
- `diameter_avps(path, session_id=None, imsi=None, command_code=None, frame=None, filter=None, detail="key", max_avps=200, limit=20)`: the AVPs of paired Diameter transactions. `key` gives result codes, procedure flags with bit names (ULR, CLR, PUR, PUA, IDR, ...), Cancellation-Type, RAT-Type, Gx request type and rule reports, and a Subscription-Data digest with one line per APN; `full` gives the whole AVP tree, capped per message. Use it when a transaction row needs the why (what the HSS sent, why the MME asked).
- `gtp_sessions(path, imsi=None, apn=None, teid=None, filter=None, limit=200)`: GTPv2-C requests paired with responses by sequence number; IMSI, APN, F-TEIDs, cause, PAA.
- `gtpv1_sessions(path, imsi=None, apn=None, teid=None, filter=None, limit=200)`: GTPv1-C (Gn/Gp) PDP context signalling paired by sequence number, with APN, NSAPI, TEIDs, GSN addresses, end-user address and cause names.
- `gtp_user_plane(path, teid=None, limit=200)`: GTP-U packets and bytes per tunnel endpoint id with inner addresses.
- `gtp_tunnel_health(path, teid=None, mtu=1500, limit=200)`: user-plane health per GTP-U tunnel: inner TCP retransmissions, reordering, resets and the MSS in SYNs against the tunnel overhead and path MTU, inner and outer ICMP errors (fragmentation needed), one-way tunnels, all summed up in `issues`. Use it for slow or stalled data sessions instead of raw tshark; it ignores duplicate copies of packets, which tshark's own analysis counts as retransmissions.
- `message_rates(path, protocol="auto", interval=1.0, imsi=None, filter=None, burst_min=5, storm_min=5, limit=50)`: messages per second (or per `interval`) by name, bursts against the usual rate, and subscribers looping on one request (purge, attach or registration storms) with the gap between repeats. Relayed and retransmitted copies count once.
- `sip_dialogs(path, call_id=None, number=None, method=None, filter=None, limit=200)`: SIP grouped by Call-ID with the method chain, From/To, final status, time to final response and duration; several messages in one TCP segment are each counted in their own dialog.
- `sctp_associations(path, limit=200)`: SCTP handshake state, heartbeats, retransmissions, aborts per endpoint pair.
- `sigtran_messages(path, filter=None, limit=200)`: M3UA/SCCP/TCAP/MAP messages with global titles, operation names, IMSI and MSISDN.
- `compare_captures(path_a, path_b, imsi=None, msisdn=None, imsi_b=None, msisdn_b=None, collapse_repeats=True, limit=100)`: a working and a failing capture of the same procedure: aligned message ladders, the first divergence, the AVP/IE differences of each changed step and the timing gaps. Give `imsi_b` when the failing capture is another subscriber; with no identity every transaction is compared.
- `trace_subscriber(path, imsi=None, msisdn=None, limit=300)`: one time-ordered timeline for a subscriber across Diameter, GTPv2-C, GTPv1-C, MAP and SIP; all its passes share one time budget. Start here for "why did subscriber X fail".

## How to work with it

1. `find_identifier` on the directory, then `pcap_info` on the file it points at.
2. `trace_subscriber` for the subscriber (or `compare_captures` when a working capture exists too), then the protocol tool whose row needs more detail, using the structured filters (`imsi`, `session_id`, `call_id`, `teid`, `apn`, `method`) before raw display filters.
3. `truncated: true` means a cap was reached: narrow the filter or lower `limit` rather than retrying the same call.
4. Pairing follows what is in the file. A request whose answer was captured elsewhere is reported as `unanswered`.
